#9339. Ex-husband of Brent Sikkema sentenced to life in prison over murder-for-hire killing

Brent Sikkema at Art Basel Miami Beach Photo by Joe Schildhorn / BFA.com

The former husband of the late New York art dealer Brent Sikkema, Daniel Sikkema, aged 56, has been sentenced to life imprisonment for organising Sikkema’s murder in 2024. A federal court in Manhattan handed down the sentence on Wednesday (4 November).

In May 2026, after a two-week trial, Daniel Sikkema was convicted on charges of murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit murder in a foreign country. In addition to life imprisonment, he was sentenced to five years of supervised release.

Brent Sikkema, who was aged 75 at the time of his murder, was found stabbed to death at his home in the Jardim Botânico neighbourhood of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, on 15 January 2024. According to prosecutors, Daniel Sikkema began planning the murder in 2023 in the midst of his divorce from the dealer, with whom he had been married for around 15 years and shared a son.

As the couple’s divorce proceedings became more acrimonious, Daniel Sikkema, who holds dual US and Cuban citizenship, recruited the Cuban national, Alejandro Triana Prevez, as the hitman. On the night of the murder, Prevez entered the late Sikkema’s residence and stabbed him 18 times. Prevez subsequently received $5,000 from Daniel Sikkema and was promised further payments.

Prosecutors said Daniel Sikkema made 11 payments to Prevez and Prevez’s partner in Cuba, using the identities of unwitting friends, employees and family members to conceal the transactions. Prevez was arrested by Brazilian authorities four days after the murder at a gas station on the side of the highway in the state of Minas Gerais, around 600 miles from Rio de Janeiro. He had stolen cash and jewellery in his possession. His case is being handled separately by a Brazilian court.

Brent Sikkema was born in 1948 in Morrison, Illinois, and studied at the San Francisco Art Institute before beginning his career. In the early 1990s, he founded Wooster Gardens in SoHo, moving the gallery to Chelsea in 1999. The business became Sikkema Jenkins & Co in 2003 following the involvement of Michael Jenkins and Meg Malloy.

The gallery is now known as Sikkema Malloy Jenkins and continues to operate in Chelsea. It has championed the work of artists including Kara Walker, Vik Muniz, Sheila Hicks, Jeffrey Gibson and Arturo Herrera. A representative for Sikkema Malloy Jenkins told The Art Newspaper that the gallery will not be providing any statement regarding the conviction or sentencing.

#9338. Your Prototype Is Not Being Honest With Your Users (And Here’s How To Fix It)

Eric is a Creative Technologist at ProtoPie, where he pushes the boundaries of no-code prototyping. With a background in FinTech UX design, he brings firsthand … More about Eric ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at ProtoPie who help users turn their ideas into highly interactive animations and prototypes for mobile, desktop, web, and IoT. Thank you!

There’s a moment in almost every usability session where a participant pauses at the login screen, types something, and glances up: checking whether they’re “doing it right.” That pause is a clear sign. They’ve already clocked that this isn’t a real app, and every data point collected after that moment is filtered through that awareness.

In financial product testing, the problem is sharper. Finance users are trained to notice when something feels off: a balance that doesn’t add up, a field that accepts anything. When a banking prototype skips real authentication, participants don’t just disengage; they stop mid-session to flag it. The team walks away with findings that reflect how users behave in a demonstration, not in a real product.

The fix is narrower than you’d think. Identify the moment where participant trust is established and make that interaction real. In a banking app, that moment is the login.

This tutorial builds it: credentials that validate, a live error state, and a biometric animation that feels native — no code required.

The login flow, built around Pie Bank, a mobile banking prototype, includes functional text inputs, a masked password field, credential validation, a live error state, and a Face ID animation timed to feel indistinguishable from iOS.

In Figma, open the ProtoPie plugin with your login frame selected and choose Scene when exporting. Flattened collapses everything into a single image; Scene preserves your layer hierarchy so every element arrives in ProtoPie as a separate, targetable layer.

Before moving on: rename every layer meaningfully. “Input Username” not “Rectangle 14”. You’ll reference these names in formulas: vague names compound into real time lost.

ProtoPie’s native Input layer accepts real keyboard entry: participants type actual text, not tap a placeholder. Go to Text  → Input, drag an Input layer onto your canvas, and nest it inside your username field group. Match it visually: placeholder text Username, background fill and font to match your design.

Hit preview. Click the field. Type. That’s the prototype starting to behave like an app rather than depicting one.

Rename this layer Input Username, duplicate it, and nest the copy inside your password field group.

On the duplicated layer, change placeholder text to Password and set Type to Text Password. ProtoPie handles the masking: no custom logic needed.

Preview both fields: username shows text, password shows dots. It already feels real, and you haven’t written a single condition.

Add a new scene, even a blank one. The most common sequencing mistake in ProtoPie is trying to wire a navigation response before a destination exists. Create it first.

Select Log In, add a Tap trigger, set response to Jump, target your dashboard scene, transition Slide in from right to left.

Preview and tap. It navigates: but for any input, including nothing. The prototype is still lying. The next two steps are the fix.

At the bottom-left of ProtoPie, add two Text type variables: username and password. Bind each to its input layer with a formula:

Enable the debug icons: green overlays will show live variable values as you type. When you see your keystrokes appear in real time, the binding is confirmed.

Go back to the Tap trigger on the login button. Add a Condition with two rules, both must be true:

Move the Jump response inside this condition. Wrong credentials, empty fields, wrong format: none get through. Participants now have to actually log in. That single constraint changes the texture of every test session that follows.

Find your error message layer, rename it Error Text, set initial opacity to 0. Add a second condition (the inverse of the first), and inside it, a Change Property response setting Error Text opacity to 100.

Wrong credentials: error appears. Correct credentials: dashboard. Two outcomes: which is what makes this testable, not just demonstrable.

Go to Media, drag a Lottie layer onto canvas, load your Face ID file, and position it off-screen above the iPhone frame. On your Login with Face ID button, add a Tap trigger (rename it Tap Face ID) with four responses in sequence:

Without delays, all four responses fire at once and the scene jumps before the animation plays. Add offsets:

Enable Reset selected scenes on Jump: without it, navigating back leaves the animation stuck at Y: 60.

Preview: tap Face ID, animation drops in, plays, screen transitions. A biometric login indistinguishable from the real thing.

When authentication actually works, the error state becomes a genuine research touchpoint: do users understand the message, do they retry, do they reach for Face ID instead? These are questions a faked login can’t answer.

In stakeholder reviews, the flow speaks for itself. In engineering handoff, the interaction panel documents the behavior (conditional logic, variable bindings, timing) so engineers see intent, not interpretation.

This is why FinTech teams invest in login fidelity even when the login isn’t the feature being tested. It’s where participant trust is established. Get it right, and everything downstream produces better signal.

This tutorial is part of the FinTech Prototyping with ProtoPie series on the ProtoPie blog. The series builds Pie Bank from the ground up across four chapters, covering the dashboard, money transfer logic, and camera integration. If this tutorial was useful, the rest of the series goes further.

#9337. How Psychological Flexibility Can Help Us Belong

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

Six ways to move toward connection—even when you feel anxious, awkward, or left out.

The key to belonging may be more within your reach than you think. You don’t need to become more interesting, more confident, or less awkward. You may simply need to become more psychologically flexible.

Psychological flexibility is your capacity to stay present, open to your inner experience, and engaged with what matters to you—even when things feel uncomfortable. Researchers have been studying this capacity for decades, and it turns out that when you are more psychologically flexible, you are not only less likely to struggle with anxiety and depression, you are also more capable of pursuing what matters to you. That might mean repairing  strained relationships, joining the exercise class you feel anxious about, or starting the book club you know would bring more conversation and connection into your life.

Our sense of belonging may be shaped, at least in part, by how we respond to the difficult thoughts and feelings that arise when we reach for connection.

A recent study of more than 16,000 undergraduate students at 104 U.S. colleges and universities found that greater psychological flexibility was associated with a stronger sense of belonging. The study does not prove that flexibility causes belonging, but it points to something hopeful: Our sense of belonging may be shaped, at least in part, by how we respond to the difficult thoughts and feelings that arise when we reach for connection.

Emotional flexibility is your capacity to make room for the range of feelings that can come with being part of a group—whether you’re feeling left out, awkward, or nervous—without becoming overwhelmed by those emotions or needing to suppress them.

Meeting new people can feel awkward, getting past small talk can be tedious, and encountering people with different views can sometimes be irritating.

Sometimes our emotions give us important information. Maybe you are dreading that work event because there’s heavy drinking, and it doesn’t align with your values. That discomfort may be worth listening to. At other times, feeling uncomfortable is simply part of the experience. Meeting new people can feel awkward, getting past small talk can be tedious, and encountering people with different views can sometimes be irritating.

Try this small emotional flexibility practice: Imagine placing the feelings you’re having about a social situation into a backpack. How do you want to carry them? Do you want to shift the weight from side to side? Find someone to help you carry it?  Or perhaps offer yourself some self compassion along the way? You may not get to decide what is inside the backpack, but you can decide how you carry it into your next interaction.

Every so often, look inside. Do these feelings have useful information for you? Do they  need care or attention? If not, adjust the straps and bring them along.

Your mind can be the world’s worst co-pilot when it comes to social situations. It compares you to others, judges you, makes negative predictions and sometimes is just plain mean.

Cognitive defusion is the practice of stepping back from our thoughts rather than automatically treating them as facts.

In Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), cognitive defusion is the practice of stepping back from our thoughts rather than automatically treating them as facts.

Before entering a social event, write down some of the thoughts you’re having. Just noting a thought is a thought, helps you get some space from it. You get to decide if you want to take your mind’s advice, or just say thank you and move on.

Try this  cognitive defusion practice: When unhelpful thoughts return, try responding: “Thank you, mind. I know you are trying to help me. And I’ve decided to do this.”

The goal is not to get rid of the thoughts. It is to stop allowing them to make all your social decisions.

When we feel as though we don’t belong, we often see ourselves through a narrow lens: I am not good at conversation. I am the only person who doesn’t know someone here. I never make a good first impression.

You know you are limiting yourself when you use phrases like: I am, I always, I never, I am the only one who…

You know you are limiting yourself when you use phrases like:

I am, I always, I never, I am the only one who…

These kinds of statements can make a passing experience feel like a permanent part of who we are. But pretty much everyone has felt socially awkward at one time or another, and nearly everyone longs to belong. And chances are, you aren’t always this way.

Try this self-flexibility practice: When you notice a  narrow view of yourself taking over, see whether you can become more flexible with your idea of “me.” Can you notice someone else who may be feeling similarly? Can you recognize a way that you are already connected—through your nervousness, or simply by sharing this moment? And can you see yourself as someone who isn’t defined by  “always” and “never”? What changes when you make room for sometimes instead?

In ACT, values describe how you want to show up in your life. They are qualities of action— such as courageously, warmly, playfully, honestly, or presently.

Before entering a social situation, try this values practice. Ask yourself:

If I already felt like I fit in, how would I act?

These questions help you identify how you want to participate and connect with others. You don’t have to wait until you feel confident or included. In fact, the more you act in alignment with your values, the more you may begin to experience yourself as someone who already belongs.

Social anxiety has a way of pulling our attention inward. It shines a spotlight on how we look, whether we’re stumbling over our words, or what might go wrong next.

Try being more flexible with your attention. Notice your feet on the floor, listen to what the other person has to say, or take in the group as a whole. Shifting your focus like this can help you become less caught up in self-consciousness and more aware of what’s happening around you. There’s more to the scene than the words you are saying.

Try this attentional flexibility practice: When you notice yourself getting caught up in comparison or self-judgment, try shifting your attention. What are five things you see? What are four things you hear? What are three things you care about? What are two people you want to meet? What is one thing that matters most to you right now?

When you feel the longing to belong, try acting on it in a small way.

We build belonging one small connection at a time.

When you feel the longing to belong, try acting on it in a small way. At the grocery store, strike up a conversation with the person grabbing lettuce next to you (“What salad are you making?”) At school pickup, get out of your car and wait with other caregivers (“Who’s your kid?”). If you are waiting for a yoga class to start, talk to the person next to you (“Have taken this class before?”) If  someone is sharing the space with you, you already have something in common. It takes courage to make that move, but small gestures like these can open the door to meaningful connections over time.

Use your other psychological flexibility skills to support you! Make room for discomfort, step back from unhelpful thoughts, shift your attention away from self-judgement, broaden your perspective,  and remember why you want to connect in the first place.

Psychological flexibility offers you a greater range of ways to respond, even when you feel like you don’t quite fit in. You can make room for anxiety, step back from your mind’s commentary, widen your sense of self, orient toward your values, return to the present, and make one small move toward connection.

Try out some of these skills, and you will notice, belonging is something you co-create, one flexible move at a time.

Diana Hill, PhD is a clinical psychologist, international trainer and sought-out speaker on Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) and compassion. Host of the Wise Effort podcast, author of The Self-Compassion Daily Journal, and co-author the ACT Daily Journal. @drdianahill

#9336. Algorithmic Theming Engines: Building Self-Correcting Color Systems With `contrast-color()`

Durgesh Rajubhai Pawar is a freelance developer dedicated to building high-performance, accessible web applications. He specializes in orchestrating complex … More about Durgesh ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

The HTTP Archive Web Almanac has been tracking color contrast failures for years. The numbers have barely moved. After half a decade of design system tooling, accessibility linters, and entire JavaScript libraries dedicated to computing readable text colors, 70% of websites still fail basic WCAG contrast checks in 2025. The WebAIM Million paints an even grimmer picture — 83.9% of homepages flagged for low contrast text in 2026, up from 79.1% in 2025. The rate improves by maybe a few percentage points per year on one benchmark and actually gets worse on another. That’s not progress — that’s proof that relying on runtime JavaScript for something this fundamental doesn’t scale across the open web. We didn’t need better libraries. We’ve needed better CSS.

The contrast-color() function is that better CSS. One declaration. The browser runs the contrast math during style computation, before the page paints, and hands you the right text color. No library, no build step, no hydration flash.

Note: If you’ve seen it called color-contrast() in older articles and spec drafts — that name was changed, and the old syntax no longer works in any browser.

The Level 5 version is simple. You give it a color. It gives you back black or white, whichever has more contrast against your input.

Change --brand-color to neon green, text goes black. Change it to midnight navy, text goes white. Swap themes at runtime via JavaScript and the text adapts instantly — no event listeners, no recalculation.

A few things to know about the current version:

Meet Smashing Workshops on front-end, design & UX, with practical takeaways, live sessions, video recordings and a friendly Q&A. With Brad Frost, Stéph Walter and so many others.

This function lives across two specifications. That’s unusual and worth understanding.

CSS Color Level 5 defines what browsers ship today. One color in, black or white out. The algorithm is deliberately marked “UA-defined”, meaning the browser decides what math to use internally. Right now, every engine uses WCAG 2.x relative luminance. But that “UA-defined” label isn’t accidental — it’s a planned escape hatch.

You’ll see APCA (Accessible Perceptual Contrast Algorithm) mentioned a lot in this context. APCA models how human eyes actually perceive contrast, factoring in font weight, spatial frequency, and ambient light — a genuine improvement over the WCAG 2.x formula. By not locking “use WCAG 2.x” into the Level 5 spec, browser vendors could swap to APCA later without breaking any existing code. If the spec had shipped with a wcag2() keyword as the default, every site using it would’ve been stuck on the old math permanently.

But APCA’s future is far less certain than the hype suggests. Adrian Roselli’s “WCAG3 Contrast as of April 2026” lays out the current situation clearly: APCA was pulled from the WCAG 3 working draft in mid-2023 after failing to gain enough Working Group support. The WCAG 3 spec currently says the contrast algorithm is “yet to be determined,” and the standard itself may not be finalized until 2030 or later. Roselli also filed a Chromium issue in May 2024 asking for the “Advanced Perceptual Contrast Algorithm” experiment flag to be removed from DevTools entirely, arguing that the implementation is outdated and risks misleading developers into thinking APCA is further along — or more official — than it actually is. That issue is still open.

None of this means APCA is dead. The research behind it is peer-reviewed and substantive, and its creator has noted that colors passing APCA guidelines greatly exceed WCAG 2 minimums in the vast majority of cases. But right now, there is no guarantee APCA will be the algorithm that replaces WCAG 2.x — and that uncertainty matters for contrast-color(). If a different algorithm wins out, or if WCAG 3 adopts something entirely new, the “UA-defined” label means browsers can adapt without breaking your code. It also means the Level 6 features — candidate color lists, target ratios, the tbd-fg/tbd-bg keywords — are all designed around an algorithm that may or may not materialize in its current form.

CSS Color Level 6 adds the extended syntax — candidate color lists and target contrast ratios:

The browser would evaluate each candidate left to right and pick the first that meets the 4.5:1 AA threshold. The tbd-fg and tbd-bg keywords indicate whether the base color is foreground or background, which matters for directional contrast models like APCA. This is all Working Draft territory — doubly so given APCA’s uncertain status. Use the Level 5 version for now.

This one’s in better shape than most new CSS features. All three major engines have shipped it in stable releases: Chrome 147 (April 2026), Firefox 146, and Safari 26.0. It reached Baseline Newly Available status in April 2026. Check caniuse for the full version matrix. All three engines pass the Web Platform Tests for contrast-color(), which means the edge cases (e.g., tie-breaking logic, color space conversion, syntax parsing) behave the same across browsers.

The raw global support percentage on caniuse looks low, but that mostly reflects enterprise browsers and people who never update. If you’re reading this, your browser almost certainly supports it already.

Progressive enhancement is straightforward using @supports:

Older browsers get white text with a dark shadow for legibility. Supporting browsers get the native calculation. Nobody sees broken text.

One thing to watch for: automated accessibility scanners (Lighthouse, Axe, etc.) can’t evaluate text-shadow. They only look at the computed color against background-color. So the fallback will still get flagged as a contrast failure in CI/CD pipelines, even if the shadow makes the text perfectly legible to human eyes. If your team runs automated a11y checks, you may need to allowlist that specific rule or add a comment explaining why the flag is a false positive.

This can trip people up: “I used the contrast function, so my site passes accessibility checks now, right?”

Mathematically? Usually yes. There is a persistent myth that for certain “mid-tone” backgrounds, both black and white fail the standard WCAG 4.5:1 AA ratio. That’s mathematically false. Under the WCAG 2.x relative luminance formula, there is absolutely no background color where both pure black and pure white fail AA. One (or both) will always pass.

Take #2277d3 (a medium blue). It sits right on a mathematical knife-edge where both black and white actually pass AA (both hit roughly 4.58:1). contrast-color() will hand you whichever has the slight mathematical edge.

But here is the actual gotcha: the WCAG 2.x math has known perceptual blind spots. That same #2277d3 with black text mathematically passes AA, but to human eyes, it can be incredibly difficult to read. contrast-color() gives you mathematical compliance, which is great for automated audits, but that doesn’t always equal perceptual accessibility. (This is exactly why APCA exists and why the spec was designed to let browsers swap algorithms later.)

Furthermore, if you’re aiming for the stricter WCAG AAA standard (7.0:1), a true dead zone does exist. For backgrounds with a luminance between roughly 10% and 30%, neither black nor white will hit 7:1. In those cases, contrast-color() can’t save you — it just hands you the “least bad” failing option.

If you’re animating a background from white to black on hover:

The background fades smoothly over one second. But because the Level 5 output is a discrete value (black or white), the text color can’t be interpolated. It snaps.

And here is the visual gotcha: the snap doesn’t happen halfway through. If you’ve been building themes for a while, you probably have muscle memory from the old Sass days, where we checked if lightness($bg) > 50%. That relied on HSL lightness, where 50% is the geometric midpoint.

But WCAG 2.x relative luminance is a non-linear scale. Under the WCAG formula, the mathematical tipping point — where black and white have identical contrast against the background — actually occurs at approximately 18% relative luminance (specifically ~17.9%).

Because of that, the visual behavior during a white-to-black fade is heavily skewed. The text doesn’t snap in the middle. It stays black for the vast majority of the animation, only snapping to white at the very tail-end of the transition when the background gets extremely dark. It’s a jarring, late hard cut.

You might assume transition-behavior: allow-discrete fixes this. It doesn’t. allow-discrete does not fix the jarring visual experience because it cannot interpolate a binary output; it only shifts the timing of the hard snap to the 50% mark of the animation duration. If you need smooth text color transitions, you’ll have to layer color-mix() or manage the crossfade yourself.

If the background is a perfect middle gray where both black and white produce identical contrast ratios, the spec has a hardcoded tiebreaker: white wins. Not a big deal in practice, but worth knowing if you’re debugging gray palettes and the text isn’t doing what you expect.

The function takes a flat value. You can’t pass it a gradient or a url(). contrast-color(linear-gradient(...)) is a parse error. If your background is a photo or a complex gradient, you still need JavaScript or manually color-pick for overlay text.

Pass a semi-transparent color, and the browser blends it against an assumed opaque canvas (usually white) before running the contrast math. It’s not ignoring your alpha channel — it’s compositing it. But the result might surprise you if you expected the function to “see through” to whatever’s actually behind the element.

If a user enables Windows High Contrast, the forced-colors: active media query kicks in and the browser aggressively overwrites author-defined colors. contrast-color() bows out — forced system colors like CanvasText take over completely. You don’t need to write manual media queries to undo your contrast logic; the browser handles the hierarchy.

Black or white sounds limiting, but once you feed that output into other CSS color functions, you can build an entire component palette off a single custom property.

Pure black text on a vibrant card looks fine. Pure white on a coral card can feel flat. What if the contrast text was a very dark or very light tint of the background color instead?

Kevin Hamer explored related territory in his CSS-Tricks piece “Approximating contrast-color() With Other CSS Features”, where he used OKLCH lightness and round() to approximate the black/white switch without contrast-color() — essentially oklch(from round(1.21 - l) 0 0). That’s a polyfill strategy: get the binary light/dark decision working in browsers that don’t support the native function yet. What we’re doing here is different — we start with contrast-color()’s native output and then enrich it by injecting the background’s own hue:

When contrast-color() returns white, l is 1 (full lightness). When it returns black, l is 0. By pulling the background’s hue back in and adding a touch of chroma, you get text that reads as a deep dark indigo or a pale icy indigo instead of generic black/white. Hamer’s approach gives you the black/white decision without browser support; this one takes the decision the browser already made and gives it personality.

Fair warning: By tweaking the lightness and chroma of the black/white output, you can push a borderline contrast ratio into failing territory. Always run your tinted output through an accessibility linter before shipping.

Also worth noting: This example chains two very modern features — contrast-color() and oklch(from ...). If either one isn’t supported, the entire declaration fails silently. Your @supports block needs to test for both:

Similar idea, simpler API. Mix the sharp black/white output back into the background to soften it:

One custom property driving text, border, and potentially box-shadow or outline. Change --alert-color and the entire component recalculates.

This pattern also works well for ::placeholder text, which is a common pain point in dynamic theming. Placeholder text should be readable but visually softer than the input’s main text — color-mix() with contrast-color() gets you there:

50% mix gives you a muted but legible placeholder that adapts automatically to whatever background the input sits on.

For apps that support system light/dark mode:

When the operating system switches to dark mode, --surface resolves to #121212, and contrast-color() returns white. No media queries, no JavaScript theme detection. The whole chain resolves natively.

The practical payoff: every one of these libraries existed because CSS couldn’t do contrast math. If you’re only using them for readable-text-color selection, you can pull them out of your runtime entirely:

You might still need these for generating complex color scales, but the contrast-for-readability use case is now covered natively.

Beyond bundle size, there’s a performance angle that’s easy to overlook. Those JavaScript libraries don’t just cost you network bytes — they run on the main thread. Every time a theme changes or a component mounts with a dynamic background, your JS has to parse the color, compute luminance, decide black or white, and write the result back to the DOM. That’s main-thread work competing with layout, event handlers, and everything else your app is doing. contrast-color() moves all of that into the browser’s native style computation phase — heavily optimized C++ that runs before paint. For apps with lots of themed components, that’s a real difference in responsiveness.

There’s also a subtle bug that goes away: hydration flash. In React or Vue SSR apps, the server renders HTML without JavaScript. The client then hydrates, running JS to calculate contrast and inject the correct text color. For a brief window between initial paint and hydration, the text is either invisible or the wrong color. Moving contrast into CSS eliminates that entirely — the browser resolves the correct color during the initial paint, before JavaScript loads.

Sass era. You’d write a function that checked lightness($bg) > 50% and returned black or white at compile time. Worked for static themes. Completely useless for user-picked colors, CMS palettes, or dark mode, because the output was baked into the CSS file and could never change at runtime.

The variable toggle hack. When CSS custom properties shipped, people got creative. GitHub used a version of this for their issue label picker — splitting colors into --r, --g, --b channels, calculating Rec.709 luminance inside calc(), multiplying by negative infinity, and clamping to 0 or 1. It worked. It was also unreadable, unmaintainable, and would break silently if you got one parenthesis wrong. (Kevin Hamer’s OKLCH-based approximation is the most elegant version of this lineage — cleaner math, better perceptual alignment — but it’s still a workaround for a function that now ships natively.)

contrast-color() replaces all of these approaches with a single function call. And because the spec lets browsers upgrade the underlying algorithm, your code won’t need to change if and when a successor to WCAG 2.x contrast math lands — whether that’s APCA or something else entirely.

That 70% failure rate was never about developers refusing to care about contrast. It was about the distance between caring and shipping — the library, the build step, the runtime calculation, the hydration flash, the one component someone forgot to wire up. Every gap in that chain was a spot where accessibility quietly dropped out.

contrast-color() doesn’t make developers care more. It makes caring cost nothing.

#9335. A Rosefulness™ WONDER Walk to Notice the Living World

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

This simple practice you can do with kids invites you to pause with one detail in nature and let it guide a small act of care.

My daughter recently drew my attention to a flower. Her invitation to notice offers a simple starting point for this practice: follow a child’s attention and allow yourself to discover what they see. A flower, sounds in nature like a bird’s song, or sunshine moving across a leaf can become a meeting place between generations.

Awareness begins with the body and grows through attention, connection, and collective care.

In my work with Ivy Child International, I call this reciprocal teaching and learning, anchored in trust, the Mindfulness Multiplier Effect™. WONDER brings that spirit into our relationship with the living world. Awareness begins with the body and grows through attention, connection, and collective care. You can stand, walk, roll, sit outdoors, or peer through a window. Choose a place where you can pause.

Honor the natural rhythm of your breath. Move through the six invitations below, or stay with one that speaks to you. You can always return to the others another time.

#9334. Budapest exhibition explores Van Gogh and Gauguin's artistic excursion to Montpellier

The portico of Budapest’s Museum of Fine Art

Adventures with Van Gogh is a weekly blog by Martin Bailey, The Art Newspaper's long-standing correspondent and expert on the Dutch painter. Published on Fridays, stories range from newsy items about this most intriguing artist, to scholarly pieces based on meticulous investigations and discoveries.

Explore all of Martin’s adventures with Van Gogh here.

After Paul Gauguin arrived in Arles in October 1888 to stay with his friend Van Gogh, the two artists would go out to paint together and then socialise and discuss art in the evenings over a glass of wine. Their very different personalities, however, soon led to tensions. Living together in the confines of the Yellow House and sharing a small room as a studio, they began to row. As winter approached, and the weather made it impossible to work outside, the situation only worsened.

In mid-December, in an attempt to clear the air, Gauguin suggested that they should make a trip to Montpellier, 70 km west of Arles. Their goal was to visit the Musée Fabre, renowned for its fine collection of paintings.

The artistic result of this trip forms a central part of a major exhibition on Gauguin which opened this week at Budapest’s Museum of Fine Arts. Bonjour Monsieur Gauguin: The Circles of Post-Impressionists and Symbolists (until 28 February 2027) provides a wide-ranging exploration of the art of Gauguin and his associates. The show’s title comes from a key painting by the artist inspired by the Montpellier visit, Bonjour Monsieur Gauguin (late 1889).

Paul Gauguin’s Bonjour Monsieur Gauguin (late 1889)

Hammer Museum, Los Angeles (photograph The Art Newspaper)

Van Gogh and Gauguin travelled from Arles to Montpellier by train, which took around four hours. Although it has long been assumed that they made a day trip on either 16 or 17 December 1888, it is arguably more likely that they spent the night there and stayed for both days. The Musée Fabre had over 800 paintings on display, so they would surely have wanted time to savour the works. Many of the finest pictures were French, given by Alfred Bruyas, a local collector and patron of Gustave Courbet.

Gustave Courbet’s Bonjour Monsieur Courbet (1854)

For Gauguin, the highlight of the museum was Courbet’s Bonjour Monsieur Courbet (1854). This landscape composition includes the figure of Courbet himself, laden with his equipment and holding a walking pole. He is greeting Bruyas, who is accompanied by a bowing servant.

Gustave Courbet’s Bonjour Monsieur Courbet and Gauguin’s Bonjour Monsieur Gauguin in the Budapest exhibition

Gauguin, who was impressed with the Courbet, painted a work in response, a year later, in the Brittany fishing village of Le Pouldu. The main figure in this work is Gauguin himself, facing a Breton woman on the other side of a gate.

Superficially, the Gauguin painting bears little resemblance to the Courbet. Stylistically, Courbet’s smoothly painted picture contrasts with Gauguin’s rough brushwork. The compositions appear to have little in common, other than showing an artist encountering other people—and being greeted with a “good day” (and, incidentally, both scenes also include a dog).

The moods seem very different. Courbet appears thrilled to greet his patron and friend. Gauguin’s encounter with the Breton woman, however, is fleeting, as they happen to pass each other at a gate. The Budapest exhibition’s lead curator, Judit Geskó, sees the Gauguin picture as representing “the artist as a solitary wanderer”.

But despite the differences, Gauguin’s decision to entitle his work as he did shows that he was directly acknowledging the source of his inspiration, the Courbet. Gauguin’s title is actually inscribed on the painting, in the lower-left corner.

Gauguin made two versions of his composition: the one on loan to Budapest from the Hammer Museum in Los Angeles and the other (which was unavailable for borrowing) at the National Gallery in Prague. The Hammer picture, which was the original, was created to display on the dining room door in the small inn where he was staying in Le Pouldu.

As for Van Gogh, the Dutchman was particularly struck in the Musée Fabre by the portraits by Courbet. These included a self-portrait, The Man with the Pipe (around 1849), which may well have inspired Van Gogh one month later to paint his Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear and Pipe (January 1889).

Bruyas was depicted by a range of artists and these portraits were also much admired by Van Gogh in the Montpellier museum. Vincent described Bruyas’ appearance to his brother Theo as “a gentleman with a beard, red hair, who looks damnably like you or me”.

Postcard of Musée Fabre, Montpellier (1905)

Both Gauguin and Van Gogh were great admirers of Courbet, who was very well represented in the Musée Fabre. Although they agreed about Courbet, their tastes for other artists were often rather different. Vincent wrote to Theo that their artistic discussions in Montpellier had been “excessively electric”. He explained: “We sometimes emerge from it with tired minds, like an electric battery after it’s run down.”

Despite these animated discussions, the inspirational visit seemed a success. Vincent reported back to Theo the day after their return that in the museum they had been “right in the midst of magic”. He added: “Gauguin said to me this morning, when I asked him how he felt: ‘that he could feel his old self coming back’, which gave me great pleasure.”

Sadly, the reconciliation did not last long: just four days later Van Gogh severely mutilated his ear. Although the trigger was probably news he had just received that Theo had become engaged (which Vincent feared would threaten his brother’s support), tensions with Gauguin were also a contributing factor.

Budapest’s Gauguin exhibition is ambitious, with 80 works by the French master and 70 by other artists. Although financial valuations for exhibitions are rarely revealed, The Art Newspaper can report that its total insurance value is €1.5bn.

Van Gogh’s Field with Irises near Arles (May 1888)

Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam (Vincent van Gogh Foundation)

The show includes three works by Van Gogh: the landscape painting Field with Irises near Arles (May 1888, Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam) and two rarely-displayed drawings from the collection of the Budapest museum, The Parsonage Garden at Nuenen in Winter (March 1884) and Haystacks (July 1888).

Van Gogh’s The Parsonage Garden at Nuenen in Winter (March 1884) and Haystacks (July 1888)

The Budapest exhibition has two Gauguin paintings dating from his stay with Van Gogh in Arles: the landscape Les Alyscamps (October 1888, Musée d’Orsay, Paris) and the portrait Madame Roulin (November-December 1888, Saint Louis Art Museum). Both of these subjects were also tackled by Van Gogh.

Gauguin’s Les Alyscamps (October 1888) and Madame Roulin (November-December 1888)

Musée d’Orsay, Paris and Saint Louis Art Museum

Among the other Gauguin highlights in the show is Sunflowers on an Armchair (1901, Bührle Collection, on loan to the Kunsthaus Zurich). This is one of four still-life paintings inspired by Van Gogh’s favourite motif—sunflowers. Gauguin painted these in the Marquesas Islands (north of Tahiti), with flowers grown from seeds he was sent by a friend from Paris.

Gauguin’s Sunflowers on an Armchair (1901)

Bührle Collection, on loan to the Kunsthaus Zurich

The museum estimates that the Gauguin exhibition could see up to 350,000 visitors, a huge number for a medium-sized European capital. However, even this won’t match Geskó's Van Gogh show in 2006, which attracted 486,000 people to the museum to see the Dutch painter's works.

Martin Bailey is a leading Van Gogh specialist and special correspondent for The Art Newspaper. He has curated exhibitions at the Barbican Art Gallery, Compton Verney/National Gallery of Scotland and Tate Britain.

Martin has written a number of bestselling books on Van Gogh’s years in France: The Sunflowers Are Mine: The Story of Van Gogh's Masterpiece (Frances Lincoln 2013, UK and US), Studio of the South: Van Gogh in Provence (Frances Lincoln 2016, UK and US), Starry Night: Van Gogh at the Asylum (White Lion Publishing 2018, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale: Auvers and the Artist’s Rise to Fame (Frances Lincoln 2021, UK and US). The Sunflowers are Mine (2024, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale (2024, UK and US) are also now available in a more compact paperback format.

His other recent books include Living with Vincent van Gogh: The Homes & Landscapes that shaped the Artist (White Lion Publishing 2019, UK and US), which provides an overview of the artist’s life. The Illustrated Provence Letters of Van Gogh has been reissued (Batsford 2021, UK and US). My Friend Van Gogh/Emile Bernard provides the first English translation of Bernard’s writings on Van Gogh (David Zwirner Books 2023, UKand US).

To contact Martin Bailey, please email vangogh@theartnewspaper.com

Please note that he does not undertake authentications.

#9333. June Is For Exploring (2026 Wallpapers Edition)

Cosima has been an editor at SmashingMag since 2013. Whenever she’s not writing articles for the weekly Smashing Newsletter, she’s probably working on a … More about Cosima ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Everyone has a creative spark in them. Some bring their ideas to life with digital tools, others capture the perfect moment with a camera or love to grab pen and paper to create little doodles or pieces of lettering. And even if you don’t think of yourself as particularly creative, who knows? There might be a hidden talent waiting to be discovered!

That’s exactly what our monthly wallpapers series has been all about for over 15 years now. It’s a chance to step away from the everyday and dive into a fun, creative project. And this month is no different!

Talented artists and designers from all over the world have once again put their skills to work, creating unique and inspiring desktop wallpapers to brighten up your screens this June. You’ll find their designs below, along with some favorites from our archives that were just too good to leave out. A huge thank you to everyone who shared their creations with us this month — you’re smashing!

If you too would like to get featured in one of our upcoming wallpapers posts, please don’t hesitate to join in. We can’t wait to see what you’ll come up with! Happy June!

“June marks the beginning of summer and the end of the semester for many colleges. When I think of summer, I think of walks along the park with my family watching ducks swimming in the lake, and swimming in our pool with my siblings. Naturally from there I put them together to create an amusing scene of a duck slowly paddling around in an inner tube.” — Designed by Emma Kim from the United States.

“The ocean covers more than 70% of the surface of the Earth, yet we know barely anything about it. Maybe June can be the month you discover something new about yourself.” — Designed by Ginger IT Solutions from Serbia.

“June is such an iconic summer month, filled with sunshine, hope, and possibilities. When we raise both hands above our heads in celebratory dance, we symbolically release our cares for the day. When we do this dance in the kitchen, we not only release but also celebrate our bodies, our souls, and nourishment we’re about to give ourselves. This digital collage represents the freedom of movement, of dance, of joyful expression, of nourishment, creativity, and hope. May we all dance in the kitchen.” — Designed by Sue Jenkins from the United States.

“June reminds me of fresh fruit and bright colors, so I decided to watercolor some fruits, and it complimented well on a blue gingham picnic table background!” — Designed by Ella Peplowski from Ringwood, NJ.

“June brings in warmer weather, so I designed a baseball-patch-inspired piece to celebrate the start of the season and the nice weather.” — Designed by Madison Evans from Scranton, PA.

“June brings summer, and it’s a great time to travel and experience new adventures! An amusement park is always a good idea, although some are best enjoyed from the comfort of your own home.” — Designed by Veronica Valenzuela from Spain.

Designed by Jayden Evans from Scranton, Pennsylvania.

“I first found this color palette and thought it was very springy, and when I think of spring I think of flowers and bees. So I wanted to create a design that incorporated both in a cute way.” — Designed by Caroline Flynn from the United States.

“Summer is hidden in the simple moments — the shimmer of crystal water, the warmth of the sun on your skin, and the calm sound of a peaceful afternoon. The warm wooden deck and soft shade of the parasol create a peaceful corner made for daydreaming. Flowers bloom, lemonade stays cold, and the sunlight dances across the pool like a golden melody. It’s the season of relaxation, happiness, and small moments that feel unforgettable.” — Designed by PopArt Studio from Novi Sad, Serbia.

“I wanted to make something in Blender, and once I made these flowers I felt like it needed something more, so I added more texture and more colors to make these flowers more peaceful.” — Designed by Caroline Flynn from the United States.

Designed by James Lucia from Covington Township, Pennsylvania.

So don’t wait, take your bike and call your loved one because happiness is greater only when it is shared. Happy World Bike Day!” — Designed by PopArt Studio from Serbia.

“In celebration of high school and college graduates ready to make their way in the world!” — Designed by Bri Loesch from the United States.

“The month of warmth and nice weather is finally here. We found inspiration in the World Oceans Day which occurs on June 8th and celebrates the wave of change worldwide. Join the wave and dive in!” — Designed by PopArt Studio from Serbia.

“Summer vibes…” — Designed by Antun Hirsman from Croatia.

“It’s summer! Go out, explore, expand your horizons!” — Designed by Dorvan Davoudi from Canada.

“I love creating fun and feminine illustrations and designs. I was inspired by juicy tropical pineapples to celebrate the start of summer.” — Designed by Brooke Glaser from Honolulu, Hawaii.

“Dream away for a little while to a land where June never ends. Imagine the ocean, feel the joy of a happy and carefree life with a scent of shrimps and a sound of waves all year round. Welcome to the world of Papa Merman!” — Designed by GraphicMama from Bulgaria.

“June 21 marks the longest day of the year for the Northern Hemisphere — and sunsets like these will be getting earlier and earlier after that!” — Designed by James Mitchell from the United Kingdom.

“June brings the start of summer full of bright colors, happy memories, and traveling. What better way to portray the goodness of summer than through an ocean folk art themed wallpaper. This statement wallpaper gives me feelings of summer and I hope to share that same feeling with others.” — Designed by Taylor Davidson from Kentucky.

“Summer is taking off with some magical ice cream hot air balloons.” — Designed by Sasha Endoh from Canada.

“In the sunset, the crabs come to the surface. That little boat can’t sail, but after seeing the crabs it gets power and finally… it sails!” - Designed by Veronica Valenzuela from Spain.

“On June 5th, we celebrate World Environment Day — a moment to pause and reflect on how we impact Earth’s health. A few activities represented in this visual include conserving energy and water, shopping and growing local, planting flowers and trees, and building a sustainable infrastructure.” — Designed by Mad Fish Digital from Portland, OR.

“Shine your light, Before the fight, Just like the sun, Cause we don’t have to run.” — Designed by Anh Nguyet Tran from Vietnam.

#9332. What Poetry Can Teach Us About Wonder: An Interview With Maya C. Popa

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

An interview with poet Maya C. Popa on attention, uncertainty, and the art of remaining curious.

We often associate wonder with extraordinary experiences, moments of beauty or awe that stop us in our tracks. But what if wonder is also a way of paying attention, one that invites us to question what we think we know and remain open to what we cannot immediately understand?

Poetry offers a particular way of exploring this possibility. It asks us to slow down, look more closely, and make room for ambiguity, uncertainty, and experiences that resist easy explanation. In doing so, poetry may have something to teach us about presence, curiosity, and our capacity to find meaning in the world around us.

What if wonder is a way of paying attention that invites us to question what we think we know and remain open to what we cannot immediately understand?

Poet Maya C. Popa has spent years exploring wonder through her doctoral research and her creative work. Her collection Wound Is the Origin of Wonder examines wonder beyond beauty and astonishment, while her newest collection, If You Love That Lady, explores the ways attention and experience can challenge our assumptions. In this conversation, Popa reflects on the relationship between poetry and mindfulness, the value of questioning our perceptions, and how cultivating wonder might deepen our connection to the world around us.

As a fellow graduate of NYU’s Creative Writing Program, I’ve had the opportunity to work with Maya over the past several years and follow the evolution of her writing. The author of three poetry collections and three chapbooks, and founder of the Conscious Writers Collective, she has devoted much of her creative and scholarly life to exploring how wonder shapes our  experience of the world.

Angela Stubbs: You’ve spent years exploring wonder both as a scholar and as a poet. Having lived with the subject for so long, how has your understanding of it changed??

Maya C. Popa: I’ve become more sensitive to how “wonder” is used conversationally, often as a substitute for admiration, surprise, or delight. It’s understandable, of course, because wonder can share qualities with the sublime or awe-inspiring. But my PhD focused specifically on the idea that wonder leads us to ask questions, which is where I think its true power lies.

My intention was to study wonder not merely through an aesthetic or critical lens, but as a fundamental human aptitude.

If we look at wonder’s etymology, it’s clear it’s not a tidy, straightforward, or uncomplicated experience. It derives from the Old English wundor, which some scholars have suggested may be related to German wunde or wound. The noun form means a surpassing or breach of the mind’s faculties, while the verb form means to demonstrate a state of admiration or astonishment, or to search for understanding or meaning. “The verb wonder,” writes scholar Daniel Fusch, “indicates an emotional response to a marvelous incident; the noun wonder indicates both the name for that response and the marvelous incident that provoked it…That is, at the sight of a wonder, we wonder; such are the beautiful complications of the English language.”

My intention was to study wonder not merely through an aesthetic or critical lens, but as a fundamental human aptitude that we could cultivate that ultimately serves as a vehicle for curiosity and empathy. Of course, I also believe it’s vitally important to live in a state of appreciation and gratitude, but wonder’s stakes and demands are psychically fascinating and deserve to be considered closely by teasing out these semantic distinctions. This allows us to fully own the power of wonder, not just treat it as another modern buzzword.

Angela Stubbs: You’ve spoken before about wonder as involving both knowing and not knowing. In the opening poem of If You Love That Lady, “At the Entrance of a Love Poem, I Hesitate,” there’s a sense that arriving at an answer can actually end the inquiry. What interests you about keeping a question alive? Is there something poetry allows us to experience by resisting the impulse to resolve or explain too quickly?

Maya C. Popa: Poems unearth and discover as they go; they are, as our wonderful Nobel Laureate Anne Carson suggests, “an action of the mind captured on a page…a movement of yourself through a thought, through an activity of thinking.” Wonder catalyzes the poetic impulse. I do think it provokes a generative restlessness that naturally seeks its shape in language.

I also believe that wonder can be passed from writer to reader.

I also believe that wonder can be passed from writer to reader. As Peter de Bolla suggests in his study of aesthetic experience, literary works of art are produced through the activity of reading. It makes sense—as we read, we’re responding in our heads as we metabolize it. Reading is inherently interactive, especially for writers.

So, to answer the question more directly, I absolutely believe in the value of keeping the question alive, and I think part of our sense of aliveness comes from that feeling of ongoing inquiry into life. Rilke advised the young poet to “Be patient toward all that is unsolved in your heart and try to love the questions themselves.” We can witness the results of our need for immediate resolution, certainty, and shortcuts everywhere in our culture. It’s at the heart of some of our greatest concerns (artificial intelligence, GLP-1s, etc.). There are an increasing number of ways around critical thinking. Sitting with, even taking as much enjoyment in the question as the solution, feels like an essential part of thinking and writing to me.

In the case of the opening poem, I wanted to begin with a self-interrogation that acknowledged the recurrence of love poems throughout history, and the ways that the beloved always seems to be situated at a distance, inviting the poet to write towards them to close the gap. Then there’s the notion, also helpfully introduced by Anne Carson, that desire requires a gap. So, this collection reflects a great deal on these questions.

I always think of Lucille Clifton saying that poems come out of wonder, not out of knowing.

Angela Stubbs: Throughout this collection, perceptions are revised: a mouse becomes a wren, a hawk moth is mistaken for a hummingbird. Do you see wonder as a willingness to discover that our first perceptions, or the stories we tell ourselves, are incomplete? Does this relate, in some way, to the writing process, which requires a similar receptivity? How do you know when to direct a poem and when to follow what it is becoming?

Maya C. Popa: I always think of Lucille Clifton saying that poems come out of wonder, not out of knowing. I value that kind of mental flexibility and capacity to revise one’s thinking or perception instead of stagnating or atrophying around a belief. That openness and capacity to evaluate and reevaluate as needed is invaluable to poets, who do this regularly throughout the process of revising. I certainly wanted to pay attention to this capacity when I noticed it in myself and deliver it on the page as precisely as I could. As a poet, I often feel I’m acting both as the lightning and the bottle that captures it at the same time.

Practically, I have to listen very closely for the deeper and more interesting questions beneath the surface of my writing as I go. What drove me to the page may not be what interests me by the end of many drafts. All of this requires me to set my ego to the side and be ruthlessly honest when something is not working, either because it isn’t rigorous or precise enough in its thinking, or it hasn’t yet found its music.

It’s rare that I’ll have a poem come together over only a handful of drafts; it’s more likely that I’m working on several poems over the course of a year or two, and many I will never share.

This requires me not to know for a lot of the time, and then, as I discover and distill what I’m doing, to make that discovery legible first to myself, and then hopefully to the reader. This takes revision in layers over many months or years. That is about the time it takes for me to really understand my own sound-sense on the page. It’s rare that I’ll have a poem come together over only a handful of drafts; it’s more likely that I’m working on several poems over the course of a year or two, and many I will never share.

Angela Stubbs: In “February Clear,” you turn from looking at the natural world toward the possibility that looking itself can change us. What is the difference, for you, between merely seeing something and giving it the kind of attention that might actually alter the person who is looking?

Maya C. Popa: I always think of the adage that we see things not as they are, but as we are. I also think that we often show up with our psyches in 12 different places at once. How often are we thinking of the thing we have to do next, the irritating conversations that we just had, what other people are doing on the internet, etc? It’s hard to stay in our own lane, and in our own moment.

[A]ttention and importance are also relayed and understood through language. If ours is significantly limited, how can we advocate for the natural world?

In that poem, I was trying to capture the experience of looking and really seeing, and acknowledging how often that isn’t the case. As someone who did not grow up with an agrarian vernacular, I also acknowledge that while my ancestors might have looked at green spaces and immediately conjured a palette of words for what they noticed, I can only name a handful of any landscape’s features. And those are mostly the obvious things: the hills, the grass, the rocks. I can’t name the kind of tree or type of grass. And this matters, because attention and importance are also relayed and understood through language. If ours is significantly limited, how can we advocate for the natural world? My friend, the extraordinary naturalist Robert Macfarlane, says that “we will not save what we do not love, and we rarely love what we cannot name.”

Angela Stubbs: We often talk about “cultivating wonder,” particularly in mindfulness and contemplative spaces, as though wonder were something we could deliberately produce. After studying and writing about it for so many years, do you think wonder itself can be cultivated, or can we only cultivate the attention, openness, and receptivity that allow us to recognize it when it appears?

If we treat wonder as being purely positive, as being in constant admiration, we will so often fall prey to our moods, which will make it hard or make it feel forced.

Maya C. Popa: I think we absolutely can and should cultivate a sense of wonder. But if we come back to its purpose as being partially to drive us to ask questions, not just to admire, I think we’re closer to the thing that actually counts, which is not taking things for granted. If we treat wonder as being purely positive, as being in constant admiration, we will so often fall prey to our moods, which will make it hard or make it feel forced.

Cultivating wonder initially involves paying attention a bit more deliberately than we usually would, before it becomes a kind of natural orientation. It’s slightly different from a gratitude practice, although it also gets us out of our sense of routine and shows us what is quite unlikely, the “marvelous singularity” of our human experience.

Rachel Carson said that “the more clearly we can focus our attention on the wonders and realities of the universe about us, the less taste we shall have for the destruction of our race,” and I stand by her thinking that wonder and humility are what safeguard us from egregious destruction. If we can wonder at the unlikeliness and distinctiveness of a human life, then we’re less likely to turn to violence. The more we develop our capacity to wonder, the greater our art, certainly, and the greater the hope that we will see our interconnectedness and protect and value each other.

Angela Stubbs is the founder of Pitch Perfect Media, a PR company dedicated to amplifying the voices of women and visionaries shaping culture and change. She holds dual MFAs in Creative Writing—one in Fiction from the Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics at Naropa University, and one in Poetry from the Creative Writing Program at NYU Paris—where her studies in contemplative education and poetics deepened her meditation practice. Angela leads heart-centered meditation offerings in Los Angeles and is currently at work on a poetry manuscript exploring memory, surrender, and the art of letting go.

#9331. How To Make Your Design System AI-Ready

Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

AI-generated prototypes often don’t deliver consistently decent results because of tiny inconsistencies scattered all across a design system. I’s decisions made but not documented, hard-coded values never cleaned up, or relying too much on AI making sense of mock-ups or design flows on its own.

Yesterday I stumbled upon a useful practical guide by Hardik Pandya from Atlassian — on how to reduce drifts, minimize mistakes, maintain context, and improve the quality of AI-generated prototypes. Let’s see how it works.

Unsurprisingly, better AI prototypes come from better data — but also from better human guidance. We shouldn’t assume that AI knows how to choose the right component and how to design with accessibility in mind. It needs priorities, a clear path on how we make decisions, design principles, examples, do’s and don’ts.

In fact, we should treat design decisions as infrastructure. That means that every time we make a decision — not just a design decision, but even a decision on how to actually prioritize our work and how we make decisions around here — it must find a path into the spec file that is then consumed by AI.

One of the useful tools to audit the quality of the design system is FigmaLint. It’s a useful free Figma plugin for auditing tokens, states, accessibility, binding tokens, renaming layers, detecting detached instances, missing interactive states and hard-coded values — and preparing the design documentation.

If you often have to work with vendors and third parties who supply you with their design systems and component libraries, that’s a great helper to have by your side — especially if you want to improve the quality of prototypes, AI-generated code, and AI-written documentation.

To ensure quality, we establish design principles, guidelines, and rules in the form of “spec files”. It’s structured Markdown files that include spacing rules, color choices, component usage guidelines, priorities, etc. AI is going to read and reuse that spec file every time it’s going to generate a prototype.

Because the spec files are text files, it’s much more cost-effective but also much more accurate, just because we don’t rely on AI recognizing or decoding patterns from mock-ups but get specific guidelines instead. In fact, extending code is often a more effective way than generating code from mock-ups.

The token layer lists and keeps updated all tokens used throughout the design system. AI always chooses from a closed set of named variables instead of inventing plausible values ad hoc.

An audit script catches what AI gets wrong. It scans the prototype and flags every hard-coded value and flags it if necessary. It can be a regular software doing that, with AI waiting for its feedback to come back.

Finally, when a design system ships updates, a sync routine flags which spec files need updating. The goal is to make sure that AI always reads up-to-date, current specs, not the ones written against an outdated version.

Ultimately, AI cannot magically resolve technical debt or design debt without proper guidance. It relies heavily on clear decisions, established priorities, and well-defined principles.

The more deliberate and precise designers are in guiding AI, the better the overall outcomes will be. This requires not just cleaning up and improving design systems but also maintaining them over time as decisions need to trickle down into Markdown files. We’ll be busy for years to come.

A primary beneficiary is the person or entity you designate to receive an asset — such as a life insurance policy, 401(k), IRA, or bank account — when you die. If you name multiple primary beneficiaries, they split the asset according to the percentages you specify. A contingent beneficiary (also called a secondary or backup beneficiary) receives the asset only if all primary beneficiaries are unable to inherit, either because they predeceased you, disclaimed the inheritance, or cannot be located.

This layered system exists because life is unpredictable. If you name your spouse as primary beneficiary on your life insurance and you both die in the same accident, the contingent beneficiary ensures the proceeds go where you intended rather than into your general estate where they become subject to probate.

You can name individuals, trusts, charities, or even your estate as a beneficiary. However, naming your estate is generally a poor choice because it forces the asset through probate, exposing it to creditors, delays, and court costs. The entire purpose of a beneficiary designation is to transfer assets outside of probate — naming your estate defeats that advantage.

When naming multiple beneficiaries, you must choose a distribution method that determines what happens if one beneficiary dies before you. This choice is critical and frequently misunderstood.

Per stirpes (Latin for "by the branch") means each branch of your family tree receives its designated share. If your son predeceases you, his share passes down to his children (your grandchildren) in equal portions. The family branch stays intact.

Per capita (Latin for "by the head") means assets are divided equally among surviving beneficiaries only. If your son predeceases you, his share is redistributed among your other surviving beneficiaries — his children receive nothing.

For most families, per stirpes is the safer default because it prevents accidental disinheritance of grandchildren. If you want surviving beneficiaries to absorb the shares of those who predecease you, per capita achieves that — but make sure that outcome aligns with your actual wishes.

Some financial institutions also offer per capita at each generation, which distributes equally among the nearest living generation first, then passes remaining shares equally to the next generation. This hybrid approach is less common but available at some custodians.

Beneficiary designations are deceptively simple forms that create binding legal consequences. The most expensive mistakes happen not from malice but from neglect.

In most states, a divorce does not automatically remove your ex-spouse from beneficiary designations on retirement accounts or life insurance policies. Federal law (ERISA) governs employer-sponsored plans like 401(k)s, and ERISA does not recognize state divorce revocation statutes. If you divorce and never update your 401(k) beneficiary, your ex-spouse can legally claim the entire balance — even if your will leaves everything to your new spouse.

Minor children cannot legally receive life insurance proceeds or retirement account distributions. If you name a 5-year-old as beneficiary, the insurance company will not release funds until a court appoints a guardian or conservator of the child's property. This process costs $2,000 to $5,000 in legal fees, takes months, and requires ongoing court reporting. Instead, name a trust for the benefit of the child or use your state's Uniform Transfers to Minors Act (UTMA) custodial designation.

If you leave the beneficiary field blank or all named beneficiaries predecease you without a contingent, the asset typically defaults to your estate. This triggers probate, adds 6 to 18 months of delay, and exposes the asset to estate creditors. Always name at least one contingent beneficiary.

Your beneficiary designations and your will can contradict each other. The beneficiary designation always wins. If your will says your daughter gets your IRA but the IRA beneficiary form still names your brother, your brother gets the IRA. Review both documents together annually.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Set a recurring calendar reminder to review every beneficiary designation once per year — ideally alongside your tax preparation. Pull statements from your 401(k), IRA, life insurance, bank accounts, and brokerage accounts. Verify that primary and contingent designations match your current wishes. This 30-minute annual review prevents the kind of outdated-beneficiary disasters that lead to costly litigation and assets going to unintended recipients.

Yes. You can name multiple primary beneficiaries and assign a percentage to each. For example, you could name three children as primary beneficiaries at 33.3% each. The percentages must total 100%.

If all primary beneficiaries predecease you and no contingent is named, the asset typically defaults to your estate. This forces the asset through probate, where it is subject to creditor claims, court costs, and delays of 6 to 18 months.

For state-law-governed accounts like IRAs and life insurance, some states have revocation-upon-divorce statutes — but not all. For ERISA-governed accounts like employer 401(k)s, federal law does not recognize state divorce revocation. You must manually update the beneficiary form after divorce to be safe.

Yes. A beneficiary can file a qualified disclaimer within 9 months of the account holder's death. The disclaimed asset then passes to the contingent beneficiary or according to the plan's default rules. Disclaimers are sometimes used for tax planning purposes.

Naming a trust provides control over how and when assets are distributed — especially useful for minor children, spendthrift beneficiaries, or blended families. However, trusts named as IRA beneficiaries must meet specific IRS requirements to qualify for stretch distributions under the SECURE Act. Consult an estate planning attorney before naming a trust as retirement account beneficiary.

A POD designation on a bank account functions exactly like a beneficiary designation. The named person receives the account balance upon your death without going through probate. You maintain full control of the account during your lifetime and can change the POD beneficiary at any time.

Primary and contingent beneficiary designations are among the most powerful — and most overlooked — estate planning tools. They transfer assets instantly upon death, bypass probate entirely, and override your will in every state. The 30 minutes it takes to review and update your designations after every major life event can save your family months of legal proceedings, thousands in attorney fees, and the heartbreak of assets going to unintended recipients.

#9329. Norfolk Coast

The Norfolk Coast is one of the UK’s best-loved and most at-risk tourist destinations. Designated an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, the region is also home to Sites of Special Scientific Interest, National Nature Reserves, Marine Conservation Zones, a Biosphere Reserve and Heritage Coast. A collection of protected landscapes, united through their biodiversity and fragility. Lantern was appointed to bring these organisations together and better define and promote their common goals to preserve, restore and enhance the local life, landscapes and wildlife of the Norfolk Coast.

We helped to define this unique destination’s strategic positioning, whilst delivering a new visual and verbal identity to promote the responsible exploration of the region, ensuring it’s here for everyone, forever.

Hiking, cycling and kayaking through protected landscapes

To fully understand what makes Norfolk so special and distinct, we embarked on a four-day immersion trip as a team. We hiked, cycled, bird watched, and conducted several interviews with local families and visitors.

It was important for us to discover the genuine essence of Norfolk and what it means for the local community and stakeholders who call it home, as well as identifying the key areas that require greater protection.

Norfolk’s coastal landscapes, seascapes and communities have rhythms like a heartbeat. They move across millennia, change with the seasons, and even differ day to day. Waterways widen and wander. Wildlife migrates and hibernates. Farmland flourishes and lies fallow. This is a living coast in perpetual motion. This is a living coast in perpetual motion. Often wild yet sometimes serene.

Our new strategy celebrates this wild, natural backdrop and all that defines it; land and sea, nature and community, they all live together in gentle harmony. And like every living thing, this delicate place deserves to be respected and protected.

Inspired by the sweeping landscapes of Norfolk’s coast and creeks we brought together the N and C of the brand name creating a unique symbol, paired with a visual language that’s full of energy and alive with nature.

Reflected through the interplay of type, image and illustration, we put the audience deep into the experience. To further reflect the landscape we directed an off-season photoshoot, encouraging sustainable exploration throughout the year.

A suite of illustrations capture key essences from our findings and strategy along with unique wildlife and nature found in Norfolk. We utilise these within patches and stamps reflecting the positive adventures we want to encourage people to experience.

#9328. How to Cope With Loneliness: 5 Mindfulness Practices to Feel More Connected

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

Feeling lonely isn't a personal failing, and you don't have to transform your social life overnight in order to feel more connected. Try these five gentle mindfulness practices.

I live in a rural area, about four miles from my nearest neighbor. My husband works away on a two-weeks-on, two-weeks-off rotation, which is fairly common where I live. The community is widely scattered, you need a car to get almost anywhere, and there isn’t a great deal of interaction between neighbors. In fact, I suspect many people don’t even know who lives closest to them.

But I want to make something clear: I’m not generally a lonely person.

Loneliness doesn’t only find people with empty calendars or empty houses. It looks different for everyone.

At school, I was labeled a “loner.” I’ve never had a large circle of friends, preferring instead the company of two or three close ones. Those friendships have lasted through the years and many birthdays. Two of my closest friends live in the UK, and we keep in touch through online chats, time difference and all.
